docs.title: Understanding ADHD: A Guidebook for People with ADHD and the People Who Care for Them
docs.text: This guidebook is a comprehensive, evidence-based resource on Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). It combines the science of ADHD with practical, day-to-day strategies, and it is written for two readers at once: the person who has ADHD, and the people who love and support them — parents, spouses, partners, siblings, and close friends. A new diagnosis lands on a whole family, not just one person. This book is for the whole family.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text:
This textbook is designed for:

  • Adults and teens who have been diagnosed with ADHD, or who suspect they have it — especially adults diagnosed late, and women whose ADHD went unrecognized for years
  • Parents of a child, teen, or adult child with ADHD — including parents learning how to support a grown daughter or son without parenting them like a child
  • Spouses and partners of someone with ADHD, now or in the future
  • Siblings, close friends, and extended family who want to understand and help
  • Teachers, coaches, and mentors without specialized ADHD training
  • General learners interested in understanding ADHD and neurodiversity

We assume our reader has no medical or psychological background. Every clinical term is explained in plain language when it first appears.

docs.title: Reading Level
docs.text: Written at a 9th-10th grade reading level for maximum accessibility, with complex concepts explained using clear language, diagrams, interactive simulations, and real-world examples.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: None. All essential concepts are explained from the ground up.

docs.title: How to Use This Guidebook
docs.text:
• Sequential reading: Work through chapters in order for a complete understanding
  • Reference guide: Jump to specific topics as questions come up — before a doctor's visit, a school meeting, or a hard conversation
  • Shared reading: The person with ADHD and a caregiver read the same chapter and compare what rang true — the book is built for that conversation
  • Educational course: Follow the structured learning path with quizzes, checklists, and activities

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this course, learners will be able to:

Remember (Knowledge):

  • Define key terms including ADHD, executive function, working memory, dopamine, hyperactivity, inattention, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation
  • List the three presentations of ADHD (inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined) and their distinguishing features
  • Identify the common signs of ADHD at each life stage: childhood, adolescence, and adulthood
  • Recall the major evidence-based treatment options and the professionals who provide them
  • Name the most common co-occurring conditions (anxiety, depression, learning disabilities, sleep disorders)

Understand (Comprehension):

  • Explain how ADHD affects brain development, attention regulation, and the brain's reward system
  • Describe why ADHD is a difference in regulation, not a deficit of intelligence, effort, or character
  • Explain why ADHD often looks different in girls and women, and why they are diagnosed later
  • Interpret what happens in a diagnostic evaluation and what a diagnosis does and does not mean
  • Understand how stimulant and non-stimulant medications work, and what they can and cannot do
  • Describe rejection sensitivity, time blindness, and hyperfocus, and why they occur

Apply (Application):

  • Use evidence-based strategies for daily structure: routines, reminders, body doubling, and externalizing memory
  • Apply communication techniques that reduce conflict between a person with ADHD and their family
  • Implement school and workplace accommodations, and navigate the process of requesting them
  • Use tools and technology (planners, timers, apps) matched to how ADHD brains actually work
  • Practice self-advocacy: explaining one's own ADHD to teachers, employers, friends, and partners

Analyze (Analysis):

  • Compare treatment options — medication, behavioral therapy, coaching, exercise, sleep, nutrition — and the evidence behind each
  • Distinguish ADHD from look-alike conditions and identify when co-occurring conditions need their own attention
  • Analyze recurring family conflicts (chores, homework, lateness, forgotten promises) to find the executive-function breakdown underneath the behavior
  • Break down a failing routine or system to find where it fights the ADHD brain instead of working with it
  • Examine how ADHD shows up differently across life stages and relationships — child and parent, student and teacher, partner and partner

Evaluate (Evaluation):

  • Assess whether a treatment plan is working, using concrete criteria and tracking
  • Judge the quality of ADHD information and products — separating evidence from myth, marketing, and social-media misinformation
  • Evaluate when to seek a professional: diagnosis, medication review, therapy, coaching, or crisis support
  • Assess caregiver strain and recognize when the supporter needs support
  • Critique one's own strategies honestly: keep what works, drop what doesn't, without shame

Create (Synthesis):

  • Develop a personalized support plan that fits the individual's ADHD profile, strengths, and goals
  • Design home routines and physical environments that reduce friction for an ADHD brain
  • Create a family communication agreement: how to give reminders, handle slip-ups, and repair after conflict
  • Build a care team and support network — clinicians, coaches, school or workplace allies, peer community
  • Compose a personal "owner's manual": how my ADHD works, what helps, what hurts, and what I need from the people around me

docs.title: Topics Covered
docs.text:
This guidebook is organized into these major areas:

  1. What ADHD Is — and Is Not: definitions, history, myths, and the neurodiversity perspective
  2. The ADHD Brain: brain development, executive function, dopamine, and the science of attention
  3. The Three Presentations: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, and combined
  4. ADHD Across the Lifespan: childhood, adolescence, college years, adulthood, and diagnosis at any age
  5. ADHD in Girls and Women: masking, high achievement hiding the struggle, late diagnosis, hormonal influences
  6. Getting a Diagnosis: evaluation, rating scales, who diagnoses, and what a diagnosis means
  7. Co-occurring Conditions: anxiety, depression, learning disabilities, sleep problems, and more
  8. Medication: stimulants, non-stimulants, how they work, side effects, and finding the right fit
  9. Non-medication Treatment: behavioral therapy, ADHD coaching, exercise, sleep, and nutrition
  10. Executive Function Skills: time, memory, organization, planning, and getting started
  11. Emotional Life with ADHD: emotional dysregulation, rejection sensitivity, shame, self-esteem, and making sense of your own history after a late diagnosis
  12. Strengths and Thriving: creativity, energy, hyperfocus, and building a life that fits
  13. School and Learning: study strategies, accommodations, IEPs and 504 plans, college supports
  14. Work and Career: choosing work that fits, workplace accommodations, disclosure decisions
  15. Family Life: supporting a family member with ADHD at any age — from parenting a child to standing beside an adult — chores and conflict, communication that works, and respecting an adult's autonomy while still helping
  16. Partners and Relationships: dating, marriage, and the caregiver-partner dynamic
  17. Caring for the Caregiver: strain, burnout, and support for the supporters
  18. Daily Systems and Tools: routines, environment design, planners, timers, and technology
  19. Self-Advocacy and Identity: owning the diagnosis, explaining it to others, community
  20. The Road Ahead: current research, emerging treatments, and living well long-term

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
To keep the book focused and safe, this guidebook does not cover:

  • Medical dosing advice or medication selection for a specific person — that belongs to the prescribing clinician
  • Diagnosis of any individual — the book explains the process but cannot replace an evaluation
  • Autism spectrum disorder in depth (it is discussed only where it co-occurs with ADHD)
  • Legal advice on disability law beyond a general orientation to rights and accommodations
  • Alternative treatments without a credible evidence base, except to explain how to evaluate such claims

docs.title: Scope and Depth
docs.text:
This guidebook provides:

  • Evidence-based coverage of ADHD science, diagnosis, and treatment, drawn from current research and consensus guidelines
  • Practical, actionable strategies for daily life, school, work, and relationships
  • Both sides of every topic: what the person with ADHD experiences, and what the caregiver can do
  • Real-world scenarios showing strategies in action
  • Interactive elements including checklists, self-assessment tools, conversation guides, tracking templates, and interactive simulations (MicroSims) of core concepts

docs.title: What Makes This Resource Unique
docs.text:
• Dual audience by design: every major topic addresses the person with ADHD and their caregivers together, so both sides read the same book and meet in the middle
  • Family-centered: written from the conviction that ADHD outcomes depend on the alliance around the person, not just the person
  • Strengths-honest: takes ADHD seriously as a disability where it is one, and seriously as a difference with real strengths — without romanticizing either
  • Non-clinical perspective: written for families, not professionals, with every term explained
  • Lifespan view: follows ADHD from childhood through adulthood, including the transitions — high school to college, college to work, dating to partnership — where support systems change hands
  • Interactive learning: combines reading with simulations, quizzes, and practical activities

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 15 chapters covering 300 concepts from the learning graph.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. What ADHD Is And Is Not - This chapter lays the foundation for everything that follows: what attention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity actually are, how ADHD is formally defined, and where it comes from.
  2. The ADHD Brain - This chapter explains how the ADHD brain works: brain development, executive function and its components, dopamine and the reward system, and why motivation behaves differently.
  3. Presentations And Everyday Traits - This chapter covers the three official presentations of ADHD and the everyday traits families actually recognize: hyperfocus, time blindness, procrastination, forgetfulness, and the inconsistency that confuses everyone.
  4. ADHD Across The Lifespan - This chapter follows ADHD from childhood through adulthood, with special attention to how it shows up in girls and women and why so many are diagnosed late.
  5. Getting A Diagnosis - This chapter walks through the diagnostic process end to end: who can diagnose, what an evaluation involves, how to prepare, and what the report does and does not mean.
  6. Co-occurring Conditions - This chapter covers the conditions that commonly travel with ADHD — anxiety, depression, learning disabilities, autism, sleep disorders — plus ADHD burnout.
  7. Medication - This chapter explains ADHD medication without hype or fear: how stimulants and non-stimulants work, what titration is, what side effects to watch, and how to track whether a medication is actually helping.
  8. Treatment Beyond Medication - This chapter surveys everything beyond medication with evidence behind it: behavioral therapy, CBT, ADHD coaching, exercise, sleep, nutrition, and mindfulness.
  9. Building Daily Systems - This chapter begins the practical toolkit: externalizing memory instead of trusting it, breaking tasks down, estimating time, using timers, body doubling, and building routines that fit an ADHD brain.
  10. Tools And Keeping Systems Alive - This chapter continues the toolkit with the physical and digital environment: visual reminders, decluttering, calendars, planners, distraction blockers, and prioritization.
  11. Emotional Life And Identity - This chapter addresses the emotional side of ADHD that rarely makes the diagnostic checklists: emotional dysregulation, rejection sensitivity, shame from years of negative feedback, and the grief and relief of a late diagnosis.
  12. School And College - This chapter covers learning with ADHD from study strategies through formal accommodations: IEPs and 504 plans in school, disability services in college, and how to actually request help.
  13. Work And Career - This chapter takes ADHD to work: finding career fit, workplace accommodations and the ADA, the disclosure decision, managing meetings and deadlines, and preventing burnout.
  14. Family Life And Communication - This chapter is where the book's two audiences meet: how ADHD lands on a family system, what the caregiver role really is, and how to support an adult family member without slipping into parenting them.
  15. Partners And Caring For The Caregiver - The final chapter covers romantic partnership with ADHD — dating, telling a new partner, the partner-parent trap, dividing the mental load — and then turns to the caregivers themselves: strain, burnout, boundaries, and support.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Chapters are ordered so that every concept appears after its prerequisites — reading in order always works. The book is also built for the two of you to read together: most chapters address the person with ADHD and their caregivers side by side, so reading the same chapter and comparing notes is a feature, not a shortcut.

Note: Each chapter lists the concepts it covers. Complete prerequisite chapters before moving to advanced ones.

Summary
docs.text: This chapter lays the foundation for everything that follows: what attention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity actually are, how ADHD is formally defined, and where it comes from. It also clears the ground of the myths — laziness, weak willpower, low intelligence — that make life harder for people with ADHD and their families. After this chapter, both readers share a common vocabulary and can tell evidence from misinformation.

docs.title: Learning Graph for Understanding ADHD
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.text:

docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: The 300 concepts of Understanding ADHD are organized into 12 categories. Each category has a TaxonomyID used in the learning graph CSV and JSON.

docs.title: ADHD Foundations (FOUND)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: FOUND

What ADHD is and is not: core terms (attention, hyperactivity, impulsivity), the formal definition, history, prevalence, causes, myths, stigma, and how to tell evidence from misinformation.

docs.title: Brain Science (BRAIN)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: BRAIN

How the ADHD brain works: brain development, executive function and its components, dopamine and the reward system, motivation, sleep, and what research actually shows.

docs.title: Presentations And Traits (PRES)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: PRES

The three official presentations and the day-to-day traits people recognize: hyperfocus, time blindness, distractibility, procrastination, forgetfulness, masking, and the inconsistency that confuses everyone.

docs.title: Lifespan And Late Diagnosis (LIFE)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: LIFE

ADHD at every age, the transitions between stages, and the story of late diagnosis — especially in girls and women, where masking and high achievement hide the struggle.

docs.title: Diagnosis And Evaluation (DIAG)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: DIAG

What a diagnostic evaluation involves, who can diagnose, how to prepare, what the report means, and the pitfalls: misdiagnosis, underdiagnosis, cost.

docs.title: Co-occurring Conditions (COMO)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: COMO

The conditions that travel with ADHD — anxiety, depression, learning disabilities, autism, sleep disorders — plus burnout, and how treatment is ordered when more than one condition is present.

docs.title: Medication (MED)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: MED

Stimulants and non-stimulants: how they work, finding the right medication and dose, side effects, practical logistics, and how to decide whether medication belongs in the plan.

docs.title: Treatment Beyond Medication (TREAT)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: TREAT

Everything else with evidence behind it: behavioral therapy, CBT, coaching, exercise, sleep, nutrition, mindfulness — and how to evaluate treatment claims that lack evidence.

docs.title: Daily Systems And Skills (SKILL)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: SKILL

The practical toolkit: externalizing memory, timers, routines, environment design, body doubling, planners, and keeping systems alive after the novelty wears off.

docs.title: Emotional Life And Identity (EMO)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: EMO

Emotional dysregulation, rejection sensitivity, shame and self-esteem, making sense of the past after a late diagnosis, self-advocacy, strengths, and the capstone: a personal owner's manual.

docs.title: School And Work (EDU)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: EDU

Study strategies, accommodations from IEPs through college disability services to the ADA, career fit, workplace disclosure, and preventing burnout at work.

docs.title: Family And Caregivers (REL)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: REL

The book's distinctive territory: how ADHD lands on a family, supporting an adult without parenting them, communication that works, dating and partnership, and care for the caregivers themselves.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
Only one element scored below full points:

  • Create Level (8/10): The outcomes are strong, but no single one is designated as the capstone. The personal "owner's manual" is the natural candidate — the reader with ADHD writes their own, and caregivers write the companion "how to be on my team" page. Naming it as the capstone would give chapter and quiz generation a clear summit to build toward.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
1. When the chapter structure is designed, make the "owner's manual" the explicit capstone project and have late chapters feed sections of it.
  2. The 20 topics are broader than the rubric's "ideally 5-10" — this is a strength for concept generation (more raw material), but the book-chapter-generator should merge related topics into 12-16 chapters rather than mapping one-to-one.

  • Skills and strategies (daily systems, school, work, communication) yield ~60-80 concepts
  • Relationship and caregiver material (family dynamics, partner dynamics, caregiver wellbeing, self-advocacy) yields ~40-60 concepts — this cluster is the book's distinctive contribution and should not be shortchanged in the graph

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text: This interactive viewer allows you to explore the learning graph for this course.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find specific concepts
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide concept categories
  • Interactive Navigation: Click and drag to explore, scroll to zoom
  • Statistics: View real-time counts of visible nodes and edges

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find concepts. Click on a result to focus on that node.

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

  4. Drag to pan around the graph
  5. Scroll to zoom in and out

  6. Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections

  7. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts (left side): Prerequisites with no dependencies
  • Advanced Concepts (right side): Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to its prerequisites
